618.author: HugoXK
618.body:
Follow-up to #245, criterion 3. PR #617 delivers the measurement harness and the per-request wire diagnostics, but the real relay-vs-direct measurement is **not** delivered: the team's bot host has no relay or model endpoint credentials.

## What is missing

Criterion 3 of #245 asks for a comparison of a relay endpoint against a direct endpoint with the same model alias, the same request body bytes, the same workload and the same concurrency, with wire latency reported separately from agent duration and token counts. The harness exists (`scripts/model-endpoint-compare.mjs`, delivered in #617 and covered by `scripts/model-endpoint-compare.test.mjs` against local stub endpoints). What does not exist is a run against real endpoints, so #245 stays open as partially delivered.

## Who can run it

Someone on an owner-hosted machine that has both endpoint URLs and their credentials. The team's bot host cannot: it has no model credentials, and this is not a code problem.

## Command (fill the placeholders)

```bash
node scripts/model-endpoint-compare.mjs \
  --model <model-alias> \
  --prompt-file <one-prompt.txt> \
  --a-name relay  --a-base-url <relay-base-url>  --a-token-env A_TOKEN \
  --b-name direct --b-base-url <direct-base-url> --b-token-env B_TOKEN \
  --requests 20 --concurrency 2 --timeout-ms 300000 \
  --out compare.json
```

`--body-file <identical-body.json>` may be used instead of `--prompt-file` when the exact request body must be reused. The script refuses two different model aliases and refuses a workload where the two bodies would differ, so a latency delta cannot come from a body change.

## What to do with the result

Paste the comparison table the script prints (p50/p90/p95 per endpoint, failures, tokens) and attach or link `compare.json` in #245. That closes criterion 3.

## Notes

- Endpoint tokens are read from the environment variables named by `--a-token-env` / `--b-token-env`; they are never written into the report.
- No repository change is expected from this issue: it is a measurement task, not a code task.

Related: #245, #617.
618.title: [Follow-up] Measure relay vs direct model latency on an owner-hosted endpoint (#245 criterion 3)

619.author: HugoXK
619.body:
## Problem

`SseFrameDecoder` in `apps/desktop/src/api/stream.ts` keeps a partial frame in memory until it sees the `\n\n` terminator. On `main` at `ca98c195`:

- `push` appends the chunk to the retained buffer — `apps/desktop/src/api/stream.ts:41-44` (append at line 42);
- `drain` re-normalizes the whole buffer with `this.buffer.replace(/\r\n/g, "\n")` and only then looks for a blank line — `apps/desktop/src/api/stream.ts:51-70` (lines 55 and 56);
- `flush` is only reached when the stream ends — `apps/desktop/src/api/stream.ts:46-49`, called from `apps/desktop/src/api/stream.ts:111`.

If a stream keeps sending bytes for a frame that never receives its terminating blank line, the buffer grows for as long as that stream stays open. Memory grows with bytes received, and because the whole buffer is re-scanned on every chunk, total work grows quadratically. While the stream is open nothing bounds it and nothing reports it; if the stream ends, the tail reaches `flush()` and is counted as a skipped frame (#616). The gap this issue closes is the **live window**. Growth needs continuing bytes after an unterminated frame — a server that merely stalls sends nothing and so grows nothing.

**This is pre-existing on `main` and is not introduced by PR #616.** #616 handled a payload that does not parse (`stream.ts:129-140`); this is a framing failure, where no complete frame is ever handed to `JSON.parse`. #616 does cover the end-of-stream case (an over-long tail reaches `flush()` and is then counted as a skipped frame), so the remaining gap is only while the stream is still open — which is the case for a live run. The decoder region is byte-identical at `ca98c195` and at #616's head.

`pump` (`apps/desktop/src/api/stream.ts:105`) is the only production consumer. The API's own writer always terminates a frame with `data: <json>\n\n` (`services/api/src/runs/index.ts`, `writeSse`), so a normal server does not trigger this; it needs a stream whose writer omits the terminator while continuing to send data.

## Expected

> Contract note: #616 merged into `main` at `5b25c260` on 2026-10-28. The skipped-frame path exists now, so this issue specifies skip-once-and-continue, not a stream-ending failure.

- The decoder's retained buffer is bounded by a constant, so an unterminated frame cannot grow memory without bound.
- On exceeding the ceiling, the decoder discards bytes up to and including the next `\n\n` — that terminator closes the oversized frame, it does not start a new one — and never hands the dropped tail to `JSON.parse`, so a crafted tail cannot be re-interpreted as a new event.
- #616 is merged into `main` (`5b25c260`, 2026-10-28), so the skipped-frame path is available: the drop is reported **once** through it (the existing "Skipped N updates that could not be read." wording), the frame is counted once, and the stream continues instead of ending. No second notice and no new error mode.
- No bytes after the drop are parsed, and no event or cursor id is taken from the dropped tail. On reconnect the client's cursor is whatever the last fully received frame set it to.
- Clean streams and frames below the bound behave exactly as today.
- An earlier revision of this issue said the drop should end the stream as a bounded framing failure, because `main` had no skipped-frame path at the time. That is no longer the contract: #616 landed, and skip-once-and-continue is what this change does.

## Repro shape (unit level)

```ts
const decoder = new SseFrameDecoder();
for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i += 1) decoder.push('id: 1\ndata: {"type":"run.started"}');
// no frame is emitted, no error is raised, and decoder.buffer keeps growing
```

Then append `'\n\n'` plus a valid frame: at `main` the retained buffer has no upper bound, and only the later terminator releases it.

## Suggested guard (sketch, not prescriptive)

- Add a `MAX_FRAME_CHARS` constant to the decoder; pick it with headroom over the largest event the API emits (live tool results are the biggest frames).
- When no boundary is found and the buffer exceeds it, discard bytes up to and including the next `\n\n` — that terminator closes the oversized frame, it does not begin a new one — never hand the dropped tail to `JSON.parse`, count the frame once, and resume parsing after it so later well-formed frames still arrive. Report it through #616's existing one-notice path; do not add a second notice or a new error mode. Advance no cursor from bytes that were not fully received.
- Optional, same change: normalize only the newly appended part of the buffer instead of re-scanning all of it on every chunk (`stream.ts:55`) — this removes the quadratic term.
- Reuse the existing wording ("Skipped N updates that could not be read.") rather than adding a second notice.

## Verification cases

1. **Endless unterminated frame** — the retained buffer stays at or below the bound; the frame is given up on, its terminator is consumed, and the stream continues, so one bad frame does not end a live run.
2. **One failure, not many** — the oversized frame is counted once and reported once through the existing notice; a stream without such a frame reports nothing; the dropped tail is never parsed (a crafted tail that would parse as JSON still yields no event and no cursor advance).
3. **Clean stream unchanged** — every frame delivered, no error (existing `apps/desktop/tests/api-client.test.ts` cases stay green).
4. **Large but legal frame** — a frame below the bound still parses fully.
5. **No cursor from unread bytes** — the drop produces no event and no cursor advance; the replay cursor stays at the last fully received frame's id, and a cap drop never hands over an id from bytes that were never fully read.
6. **No new setting** — the ceiling is a module constant, not user configuration, preserving #505's "no new setting" constraint.

## Context

Found while reviewing PR #616 at `c7d49f79` (static review, no tests run). Adjacent to #505 but a different failure class (framing vs `JSON.parse`), so it is tracked separately. Client-only; no server change and no protocol change is needed.

Out of scope, stated so it is not mistaken for covered: with bounded memory, a peer that simply stops writing still keeps the stream open forever — `running` stays true and the follow path never settles. That is a stall/liveness question, not a memory one, and it exists on `main`. This issue does not address idle or stalled streams, and it does not change the pre-existing fact that a clean close with no parsed terminal is silent on the follow path (`use-workspace.ts:892-910`: `closeRunStream` marks `terminal: true`, a run still executing server-side can look finished). That is a separate liveness/wording item, unchanged by this fix.

Owner: ScienceDiscovery Dev-1 (desktop). Labels and milestone deliberately left to the maintainer: #505 sits on `v0.3.0`, and this repo-side label write is not available to us.
619.title: [Bug] desktop: cap the SSE frame decoder buffer so an unterminated frame cannot grow without bound

622.author: HongyeZhou
622.body:
### Background

Follow-up to #96, under the backend migration tracked in #84. This issue carries forward the unfinished scope of #96 for release 0.4.0. Closing #96 is an administrative handover, not a claim that its original acceptance criteria have all passed.

Code review baseline: main at `5a86d0593a887e825d3a3da136f760b62807f797` (2026-10-28). This assessment is based on static inspection, not a fresh full acceptance run.

### Existing behavior to preserve

- Keep the existing Runner and its bwrap / Seatbelt sandbox. Do not switch to jiuwenbox or re-enable JiuwenSwarm host execution/file tools.
- Existing environment, execution and workspace functionality remains available through the legacy API behind the adapter proxy.
- Sandbox network settings already have permission-epoch rotation and persistent-kernel teardown behavior in the legacy API. Preserve and verify it rather than treating it as missing.
- Some L1 contract cases already exist, including sandbox network and package-source settings. The historical claim of 21 uncovered rows must be recalculated against current main.

### Remaining scope

- [ ] Inventory every interface row from #96, including the expanded Runner-specific environment paths. Record its current owner, downstream target, existing coverage and remaining work. Preserve the original interface scope; explicitly justify any row requiring no migration.
- [ ] Complete adapter routing and necessary adaptation for local Runner environments, environment setup/revisions, execution records/status/logs/cancellation, kernel teardown, workspace listing/files/sync/deletion, and local Runner list/detail/connect/probe. Replace reliance on the generic legacy API fallback for this scope with explicit ownership and dispatch; reuse existing implementation where possible instead of rewriting the Runner.
- [ ] Implement the required path rewriting (`/api/environments*` to Runner `/environments*`) and dispatch of `/api/runners/:id/...`, preserving authentication, request/response contracts and errors.
- [ ] Complete `agent-activity` aggregation across Runner executions/transfers, JiuwenSwarm cron/schedules and adapter-owned state, including logs and cancellation. Current main aggregates legacy API stores; that alone does not establish the requested integration.
- [ ] Trace and complete configuration persistence and propagation for sandbox network settings and package-source settings. Verify Runner behavior after saving, permission-epoch rotation and invalidation of previous sandbox authorization where required by #96; preserve existing kernel teardown behavior. Explicitly document the intended epoch behavior for package-source changes and resolve any discrepancy with #91/#96.
- [ ] Evaluate whether the `agent-activity` wrapper can be eliminated; record the conclusion and retain only necessary adaptation.

### Boundaries and dependencies

Local Runner environments, execution and workspace only. Remote-host and NPU implementation remains in #104. Coordinate shared routing/dispatch contracts with that issue without absorbing its scope. Adapter core and settings contracts relate to #87 and #91; downstream consumers include #97 and #102.

The sandbox choice is already settled: retain Runner execution and bwrap / Seatbelt.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Publish a current interface-by-interface coverage matrix for all rows inherited from #96. Each row has an L1 contract diff case or an explicit, justified "no migration needed" classification. Include write operations such as connect, probe, install, uninstall and delete, not just reads.
- [ ] Relevant execution/activity/cancellation and settings-related events have L2 golden traces, with intentional differences documented.
- [ ] Register and run E2E journeys covering environment creation and dependency installation/uninstallation, execution status/logs/cancellation, kernel teardown, workspace inspection/cleanup, and aggregated activity/timer cancellation on the JiuwenSwarm stack.
- [ ] Verify sandbox network-policy changes reach actual Runner execution, out-of-allowlist access is refused, epoch changes do not reuse previous sandbox authorization, and package-source changes affect subsequent package operations. Apply the baseline/assertion and security-case review rules from #84.
- [ ] Demonstrate that the scoped routes use the intended explicit routing/ownership rather than silently succeeding through the generic legacy fallback.
- [ ] Record the wrapper decision, candidate SHA, executed test results and any remaining gaps. Do not mark complete while inherited acceptance items remain uncovered, failed, blocked or skipped.

### References

- Original scope and discussion: #96
- Migration architecture and test layers: #84
- Current routing: `services/adapter/src/sciencediscovery_adapter/app.py`
- Current settings and activity handlers: `services/api/src/http/index.ts`
- Interface inventory and cases: `test/contract/routes.json`, `test/contract/cases/`

The migration-status document is an archived snapshot and must not be used as current completion evidence.
622.title: [Feature] Complete local Runner routing, activity aggregation and configuration migration

623.author: HongyeZhou
623.body:
## Motivation

Long-running offline computations and Agent conversations have different lifecycles. An Agent turn can finish while a training, simulation, or batch-processing task continues running. After evaluation, this is a feature-design topic about coordination between offline tasks and Agents, rather than a defect in turn completion.

This issue replaces #434 and preserves its motivating scenario.

## Motivating scenario

In the NatureBench reproduction session `93f897ca-cefe-4e7b-932d-8339cbef1459`, run `84d71b8a-77dd-42a7-bc81-15e326b14cb1` completed while a background `python run.py --instances mop_sc` computation continued. The final computation took approximately 1,587.7 seconds and produced `predictions.npy` with shape `(5693,)`.

The user had to inspect host processes and wait for the output manually. Starting another Agent run could also launch duplicate work. An Agent promising to return after a wall-clock delay is not a reliable scheduling mechanism.

## Feature scope

Design how long-running offline tasks collaborate with Agents across turns:

- Give supported offline tasks a queryable identity and lifecycle, with ownership linked to the originating session/run.
- Make ongoing computation visible even after the initiating Agent turn finishes.
- Let a later turn inspect, await, or resume coordination with the same task without starting duplicate computation.
- Define how task completion, failure, cancellation, and results become available to the user and Agent.
- Define the default turn-completion policy when a task is still running, including whether explicit detachment is required.
- Document lifecycle limits, including runtime/service restarts and the treatment of processes launched outside the supported task mechanism.

## Design decisions before implementation

- Turn completion: wait for the task, require explicit detach, or register it in the background and notify.
- Ownership and persistence: session-level versus run-level handles, and restart behavior.
- Minimum user interface: how users discover active tasks, inspect progress, and retrieve results.
- Agent continuation: explicit user-driven await/resume versus automatic completion notification or continuation.
- Delivery decomposition: build on existing execution/query/wait capabilities and split implementation into reviewable changes.

These are open design questions; this issue does not select a policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- A user starts a representative long-running computation and can distinguish Agent-turn completion from task completion.
- The same supported task remains discoverable and queryable across turns according to the documented lifecycle.
- The Agent can inspect or await that task and retrieve its final result without launching a duplicate.
- Completion, failure, and cancellation have defined, verifiable user-visible outcomes.
- The chosen turn-completion and restart policies are documented and covered by matching end-to-end scenarios.

## Related work

- #434: original report and evidence; superseded by this feature proposal.
- #439: redirected output buffering. Log buffering is a separate concern; coordinate where progress reporting intersects.
623.title: [Feature] Coordinate long-running offline tasks with Agents across turns

627.author: qingkwl
627.body:
## Problem

ScienceDiscovery has no documented path for building the backend on a native Windows host, and one CI-side script blocks Windows development outright:

- `scripts/check-architecture.mjs` builds source paths with `path.join`, which produces backslashes on Windows. `component-boundaries.mjs` is posix-only by design (it relies on `node:path` posix behavior), so its owner()/localFile() lookups fail on Windows and the architecture check cannot pass natively.

## Expected

1. `scripts/build-windows.md` documents the verified native Windows build path (install / build / typecheck), including the `core.longpaths true` requirement (in-repo paths reach ~210 chars and exceed MAX_PATH on deep clones).
2. `scripts/check-architecture.mjs` keeps forward slashes when walking the source tree, so the architecture check runs natively on Windows.

## Verification cases

### Case 1 — Windows native build

Preconditions: Windows 10/11, Node >= 22.19.0 (24 LTS recommended), pnpm.
Steps: Follow `scripts/build-windows.md` from a fresh clone (`git config --global core.longpaths true` first).
Expected / pass: install / build / typecheck all green on a clean worktree; `pnpm architecture:check` passes.

### Case 2 — check-architecture on Windows

Preconditions: Windows host.
Steps: Run the architecture check on a Windows checkout.
Expected / pass: Source paths resolve through posix-style joins; owner()/localFile() lookups succeed.

### Case 3 — POSIX unchanged

Preconditions: Linux or macOS.
Steps: Run `pnpm architecture:check`.
Expected / pass: No behavior change vs main (posix paths are already forward-slash).

## Related

- Parent: #400 (Ship the Windows and macOS desktop client)
- Verified on Windows 11 23H2, Node v24.21.0 / pnpm 11.1.2 (recorded in the guide itself).
627.title: [Feature] Windows native build support: build guide and check-architecture path fix

629.author: qingkwl
629.body:
## Problem

The repository's startup chain (`scripts/start-stack.sh`, `scripts/jiuwenswarm.sh`) is a bash-only design: it shells out to POSIX tools, assumes POSIX paths, and cannot run natively on Windows. Windows desktop development therefore has no supported way to bring up the JiuwenSwarm gateway, and every Windows workaround so far has been ad-hoc and untracked.

## Expected

A Windows-native startup foundation under `scripts/`, in the same style as the existing `.mjs` tooling:

1. `scripts/lib/stack-platform.mjs` — platform helpers the startup chain needs: port availability probes, native spawn helpers, environment/path handling that works on both Windows and POSIX.
2. `scripts/jiuwenswarm.mjs` — the Windows-native JiuwenSwarm launcher: instance config management (`.env` handling, key rotation, port allocation), progressive-tool config management, and startup diagnostics.
3. Both covered by `node:test` suites that run everywhere the existing `scripts/*.test.mjs` suites run (Linux CI included — no Windows-only APIs in the tested paths).

This is the foundation layer of the Windows start chain; the `start-stack.mjs` orchestrator builds on it in a follow-up.

## Verification cases

### Case 1 — Launcher unit tests

Preconditions: Node >= 22.
Steps: `node --test scripts/stack-platform.test.mjs scripts/jiuwenswarm-startup.test.mjs`
Expected / pass: all tests green (10 + 13 tests; verified green on Windows 11, Node v24.21.0).

### Case 2 — POSIX CI unchanged

Steps: `pnpm architecture:check` (which runs `node --test scripts/*.test.mjs`) on Linux CI.
Expected / pass: new suites are picked up automatically and pass; no behavior change for existing suites.

### Case 3 — No new platform branches outside the platform module

Steps: Inspect `scripts/lib/stack-platform.mjs` consumers.
Expected / pass: platform decisions live in the platform module; launcher code stays platform-neutral.

## Related

- Parent: #400 (Ship the Windows and macOS desktop client)
- Follow-up: `start-stack.mjs` orchestrator (stack startup, health orchestration) builds on this layer.
629.title: [Feature] Windows-native startup foundation: stack platform helpers and JiuwenSwarm launcher

631.author: qingkwl
631.body:
## Problem

When the desktop stack runs against the JiuwenSwarm backend, `services/api` currently forces `store.useEverySkillEverywhere()` on startup whenever a JiuwenSwarm instance is configured (`services/api/src/http/index.ts`, the `jiuwenSwarm` branch). The effect: every installed skill is enabled for every project regardless of what the user selects.

The desktop UI still shows per-project skill selection (settings page + per-project toggles), but under this backend the selection is stored and never applied — a silent no-op from the user's perspective.

## Expected

Per-project skill selection should keep working under the JiuwenSwarm backend, or at minimum the forced-everywhere behavior should be an explicit, documented choice rather than an unconditional override.

Proposed design direction (open for discussion):

1. Replace the unconditional `useEverySkillEverywhere()` with a configuration switch, e.g. `SD_SKILL_SCOPE` (or an equivalent settings key) with values:
   - `everywhere` (current behavior; could remain the default during migration)
   - `project` (per-project selection drives what the agent run loads)
2. In `project` mode, the run payload resolves the project's `enabledSkillIds` and passes the resolved set to the JiuwenSwarm agent session, so the selection actually drives which skills the backend loads.
3. The UI keeps showing the truth: if scope is `everywhere`, per-project toggles should be disabled or annotated accordingly (the desktop already has the components for this).

## Verification cases

### Case 1 — project scope drives loading

Preconditions: JiuwenSwarm backend configured; scope = `project`; a project with a subset of skills selected.
Steps: Start an agent run in that project; inspect the skill set the JiuwenSwarm session loads.
Expected / pass: Only the selected skills are loaded; changing the project selection changes the loaded set on the next run.

### Case 2 — everywhere scope unchanged

Preconditions: scope = `everywhere` (default).
Steps: Same as Case 1.
Expected / pass: All installed skills load, matching today's behavior.

### Case 3 — no silent no-op

Preconditions: any scope.
Steps: Inspect the settings page rendering against the active scope.
Expected / pass: The UI never shows editable controls that have no effect.

## Related

- Parent: #400 (Ship the Windows and macOS desktop client)
- This is a design discussion first; the implementation PR follows the agreed switch semantics.
631.title: [Feature] Per-project skill selection under the JiuwenSwarm backend (scope switch design)

632.author: qingkwl
632.body:
## Problem

The desktop model picker (wizard step 3 and 设置 → 模型) is currently a native `<select>` over the provider's preset list plus a separate "custom" option: picking a model means scrolling the dropdown, and entering a custom model id means switching to the custom option first and then typing.

With longer preset lists (multi-page provider catalogs), the select has no way to search or filter, and the two-step custom flow makes quick overrides heavier than they need to be.

## Expected

A combobox-style model picker:

1. Typing filters the preset list live (match on id and display name).
2. Full keyboard navigation: ArrowUp/ArrowDown to move, Enter to commit, Esc to close without changing.
3. Free-text values stay first-class: a typed id that matches no preset is offered as a custom value directly (no mode switch).
4. Opening the dropdown shows the full unfiltered list (the current value does not pre-filter it).

We have a working implementation of this component (`ModelComboBox`, a self-contained React component + its styles) running on our Windows desktop branch; it was originally built to replace a `datalist`-based picker that had two platform bugs (the list filtered itself to the current value, and the indicator sat low), but it applies equally well as an upgrade over the `<select>`.

## Verification cases

### Case 1 — search narrows, value does not

Preconditions: provider with a preset list > 10 models, one already selected.
Steps: Open the picker; observe the list; type a substring.
Expected / pass: The dropdown initially shows all presets; typing narrows the list; reopening always starts unfiltered.

### Case 2 — keyboard-only round trip

Steps: Focus the field; ArrowDown/ArrowUp; Enter; Esc while open.
Expected / pass: Selection commits on Enter, cancels cleanly on Esc (no dialog close, no value change).

### Case 3 — custom value without mode switch

Steps: Type an id that matches no preset; commit.
Expected / pass: The value is accepted as a custom model id (same validation path as the current custom flow).

## Related

- Parent: #400 (Ship the Windows and macOS desktop client)
- Design discussion first; implementation follows as a PR if the direction is agreed.
632.title: [Feature] Searchable model picker (combobox) for the desktop wizard and settings

633.author: HugoXK
633.body:
Follow-up to #617. This issue tracks **only** the CI packaging that #617 currently carries; it does not re-open the product fix in that PR.

## Trigger

Do not implement this until the maintainers answer the CI-contract question on #617 (comment `6463813036`):

- **A — accept as written**: the packaging stays in #617; close this issue with that reason and make no pipeline change.
- **B — split (our preference)**: #617 is reduced to the product fix, and one PR implements this issue.

If the answer is A, this issue is closed rather than implemented.

## Scope (only if B)

- `real-e2e.yml`: the always-run `Summarize model wire diagnostics` step and the `model-wire-summary.json` staging.
- `.ci/model-wire-summary.mjs` and its test; `prepare-real-e2e-results.mjs` staging; the `real-report.mjs` report section; `.ci/README.md`; the `ci-contract.test.mjs` expectation bump.

Out of scope: the empty-terminal-turn product fix and the wire-diagnostics fields (they stay in #617), and the relay-vs-direct measurement (criterion 3 of #245, tracked in #618).

## Merge condition

A test must exercise the real parse path: feed `[model-sse-summary]` lines as the emitters actually write them through the aggregation and staging path, and assert the resulting document. Hand-built records are not acceptance for that script.

## Context

The packaging is additive evidence — it reports model-wire failures next to research outcomes and does not add a second pass/fail gate. Splitting it keeps a default-branch pipeline change out of a behaviour fix and removes the "contract test edited to expect the change it guards" objection.
633.title: [Follow-up] #617 packaging split: stage model wire-summary in real-E2E artifacts (only if maintainers choose B)

635.author: qingkwl
635.body:
## Problem

`services/runner` has Windows-specific behavior requirements with no platform seam:

- Killing a child with POSIX signals does not tear down the process tree on Windows (#482): the runner needs `terminateTree` semantics (`taskkill /PID <pid> /T /F`), while POSIX must keep the current signal-based behavior unchanged.
- Owner-only (0600) permission semantics rely on `chmod`, which only toggles the read-only bit on Windows (#477 covers the general platform work; the runner side needs `restrictToOwner` through the facade).
- Conda environment specifics (delay-load DLL directories, the bundled m2-bash shell location, win-64 package substitution guidance) are spread over platform branches today.

PR #478 carried an earlier version of this work but was closed; this re-lands the runner-platform portion with a clean scope (runner only), a green typecheck, no unresolvable references, and real-machine Windows evidence.

## Expected

1. `services/runner/src/platform/` provides the facade: `types.ts` (adaptation surface), `index.ts` (single dispatch point), `posix.ts` (transparent passthrough), `win32.ts` (Windows implementation: `terminateTree` via taskkill, `restrictToOwner` via icacls, conda path/shell helpers).
2. Runner call sites use the facade only: `killSandboxProcess` goes through `terminateTree`; server-side 0600 semantics go through `restrictToOwner`. No direct `process.platform` branches for these concerns in consumer code.
3. POSIX behavior unchanged (signals, chmod).
4. `node:test` suites cover both adaptations.

## Verification cases

### Case 1 — Windows tree kill (matches #482 Case 1)

Preconditions: Windows host; a Node child that spawns a grandchild that stays alive.
Steps: Call `terminateTree(child)`; inspect the process list for both PIDs.
Expected / pass: Both PIDs are gone; helper returns true. **Verified on a real Windows 11 machine** with the packaged runner build: child + grandchild gone within 1s (evidence script `verify-482-case1.mjs` run recorded 2026-10-28).

### Case 2 — POSIX unchanged

Steps: Run the runner suite (`pnpm --filter @sciencediscovery/runner test`).
Expected / pass: 37/37 green on Windows with the posix passthrough; on Linux the behavior is identical to main (posix file is a passthrough only).

### Case 3 — Facade only

Steps: Inspect runner call sites for tree-kill/permission paths.
Expected / pass: All go through `platform/index.ts`; no raw taskkill / chmod outside `platform/`.

## Related

- Implements the runner half of #482 (tree-kill) and part of #477 (owner-only permissions)
- Parent: #400
- Re-lands the runner-platform portion of the closed #478 with review feedback addressed (typecheck green, runner-only scope, no internal references, Windows evidence)
635.title: [Feature] Runner OS adaptation facade (terminateTree / restrictToOwner / conda paths)

637.author: qingkwl
637.body:
## Problem

`services/api` has Windows-specific OS behavior requirements with no platform seam (#491):

- Owner-only (0600/0700) file semantics rely on `chmod`, which only toggles the read-only bit on Windows; the most sensitive files in the service (encrypted model/MCP credential master key, generated SSH private keys) are left unprotected.
- Atomic replace via rename transiently fails on Windows with EPERM/EACCES/EBUSY while antivirus scanners or search indexers hold the destination; callers currently see raw errors.
- At-rest secret protection has no Windows story at all (POSIX file permissions carry the protection; Windows needs per-user encryption).

PR #492 carried an earlier version and was closed; this re-lands the API platform facade with a clean scope (platform layer only, no consumers rewired yet), a green typecheck, no unresolvable references, and Windows real-machine evidence.

## Expected

1. `services/api/src/platform/os/` provides the facade: `types.ts` (adaptation surface), `index.ts` (single dispatch point), `posix.ts` (transparent passthrough), `win32.ts` (Windows implementation).
2. Adaptations: `restrictToOwner` (icacls owner-only ACL, SID-based grantee for locale-safety), `renameReplace` (retry with backoff on transient locks), `wrapSecret`/`unwrapSecret`/`isWrappedSecret` (DPAPI per-user encryption, identity on posix).
3. POSIX behavior unchanged (chmod, plain rename, identity wrapping).
4. `node:test` suites cover both adaptations, including a real DPAPI round-trip on Windows.
5. Consumer rewiring (secrets store, ssh-config) lands in follow-up PRs stacked on this one.

## Verification cases

### Case 1 — Windows facade behaviors

Preconditions: Windows host.
Steps: Run `node --import tsx --test services/api/src/platform/os/win32.test.ts`.
Expected / pass: 9/9 green, including a real DPAPI wrap/unwrap round-trip of a master-key-sized blob and icacls-based restrictToOwner assertions. **Verified on Windows 11 23H2, Node v24.21.0.**

### Case 2 — POSIX unchanged

Steps: Run the posix suite; on Linux CI the posix file is a passthrough by construction.
Expected / pass: posix suite green; no behavior change vs main.

### Case 3 — Facade only, no consumers yet

Steps: Inspect the diff.
Expected / pass: New files only; no existing api file is modified in this PR (consumers arrive as separate stacked PRs).

## Related

- Implements #491 (API OS platform abstraction)
- Parent: #400
- Re-lands the api-platform portion of the closed #478/#492 per their review feedback (typecheck green, platform-only scope, no internal references, Windows evidence)
637.title: [Feature] API OS adaptation facade (owner-only permissions, replace-with-retry, at-rest secret wrapping)

639.author: qingkwl
639.body:
## Summary

This issue is the **platform layer** of the Windows desktop delivery (#400): the OS-adaptation seams in three core packages that everything else builds on — process-tree termination and owner-only file semantics in the runner, atomic replace and at-rest secret protection in the api, and directory durability plus MAX_PATH-safe lock names in the cas. It also carries the Windows build guide and the one-line CI fix that makes source paths readable on Windows.

It is the platform half of the work the closed #478 carried inside an oversized PR, re-landed per that review's feedback. The runtime behavior that consumes these seams (startup chain, execution router, micromamba, fail-closed permissions) is tracked separately and stacks on this one.

## Where the packages stand today

| Package | Current state on Windows |
|---|---|
| `services/runner` | Killing a child with POSIX signals leaves the whole process tree alive (#482); `chmod 0600` only toggles the read-only bit on NTFS; conda helpers assume a Linux layout. |
| `services/api` | Atomic replace via rename fails transiently under AV/indexer locks (EPERM/EACCES/EBUSY); at-rest secret protection has no Windows story — `0600` means nothing on NTFS (#400: "model keys are stored with DPAPI" on Windows). |
| `packages/cas` | `fsync` on a directory handle is EPERM; a 64-hex lock digest overruns MAX_PATH once SQLite appends `-journal`, failing `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` with `SQLITE_CANTOPEN`. |
| Build | No Windows build guide; `check-architecture.mjs` prints backslash paths on Windows. |

## Goals

- Every package gets a `platform/` facade: `types.ts` (the surface), `index.ts` (single dispatch point), `posix.ts` (transparent passthrough), `win32.ts` (the Windows implementation), plus `node:test` suites — the structure #400 prescribes ("per-package platform adapters, win32 and darwin side by side, single entry point, module boundaries enforced").
- Consumer call sites route through the facade only; no platform branches outside `platform/`.
- POSIX behavior unchanged everywhere, by construction (passthrough).
- The api master key is DPAPI-wrapped on win32 and restricted to its owner.

## Non-goals

- Consumer-level behavior (router, environments, permissions) — separate issue stacking on this one.
- macOS/darwin adapters — same facade shape, but darwin work is its own issue.
- Windows CI jobs (same gap as #482; evidence below is real-machine).

## Root decisions

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Facade shape | `platform/` per package with a single dispatch point | #400's "Expected new components" prescribes exactly this shape; module boundaries stay enforceable by `check-architecture`. |
| CAS lock names | posix keeps the historical 64-hex digest; win32 shortens to 128 bits | Compatibility: coordination files written by main keep working on Linux; on Windows there are no existing files, and MAX_PATH headroom is required (SQLite `-journal` suffix). |
| CAS directory durability | posix fsync; win32 documented no-op | NTFS has no directory-fsync semantics; durability relies on volume-level policy. #478's review asked for the docs to state this — both languages do. |
| API secret protection | DPAPI on win32, identity on posix, self-describing blob prefix | #400: "model keys are stored with DPAPI" on Windows; no persisted blobs exist in main, so no compatibility promise is needed. |
| Runner termination | `taskkill /T /F` on win32, SIGKILL passthrough on posix | #482's design; verified end-to-end on a live child+grandchild pair. |

## Delivery

- `services/runner/src/platform/` — `terminateTree`, `restrictToOwner` (icacls), conda delay-load DLL paths and m2-bash shell location; `killSandboxProcess` and server-side 0600 semantics route through the facade.
- `services/api/src/platform/os/` — `restrictToOwner` (SID-based icacls grantee), `renameReplace` (retry/backoff), `wrapSecret`/`unwrapSecret`/`isWrappedSecret` (DPAPI); `loadOrCreateModelSecretKey` persists through the facade and restricts the key file.
- `packages/cas/src/platform/` — directory durability, `lockFileName`; versioning/workspace-lease/workspace-lifecycle route through the facade; docs (EN+ZH) note the Windows semantics.
- `scripts/build-windows.md` + `check-architecture.mjs` forward-slash fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All eight platform/secrets suites pass on a real Windows host, including a DPAPI round-trip and a tree-kill against a live child+grandchild pair.
- [ ] The cas lock name keeps the historical digest on posix (existing coordination files stay valid).
- [ ] No platform branches outside `platform/` beyond the minimal call-site hooks.
- [ ] POSIX behavior identical to main (passthrough by construction).
- [ ] `pnpm -r typecheck` green.

## Open questions

1. Should a `check-architecture` rule codify "tree-kill/signal call sites must not bypass `platform/`" (the AC3 refinement #482's triage suggested), making this enforceable in CI rather than by review?
2. Windows CI remains absent (#482 finding 4) — is a `windows-latest` job acceptable before more Windows-facing code lands?

## Related

- Parent: #400
- Runner facade implements the runner half of #482; api/cas facades re-land #477/#491 per the closed #478/#492 review feedback
- The runtime consumers (startup chain, execution router, micromamba, permissions) stack on this issue
639.title: [Feature] Windows platform adaptation facades (runner / api / cas) + build support + DPAPI secrets

643.author: qingkwl
643.body:
## Summary

This issue is the **runtime layer** of the Windows desktop delivery (#400): everything that makes the stack actually *run* on Windows once the platform facades exist — a native startup chain, an execution-provider routing layer, win-64 scientific environments, and fail-closed permission semantics for unsandboxed execution.

It implements the "Windows: an execution-provider routing layer" section of #400's execution model, and it is the runtime half of the work that the closed #478 carried inside an oversized PR. The platform seams it builds on (runner/api/cas facades, DPAPI secrets, build support) land separately as #639; this issue starts where that one ends.

## Where the stack stands today

| Area | Current state |
|---|---|
| Startup | `start-stack` orchestration and the JiuwenSwarm launcher are bash-centric; probing is slow and serial; uv trampolines break venv entry resolution on Windows; there is no packaged-stack mode for an NSIS payload. |
| Execution capability | Hardcoded to sandboxed providers (`bubblewrap`/`seatbelt`); the capability probe answers "unavailable" on Windows and nothing can execute. |
| Scientific environments | Environment provisioning assumes a Linux conda layout; no win-64 micromamba management, no starter environments. |
| Unsandboxed fallback | Nothing: without a sandbox there is no workspace confinement, no network policy, and no approval tightening — a silent security downgrade, which #400's baseline forbids. |

## Goals

- `scripts/start-stack.mjs` runs the whole stack natively on Windows (no WSL dependency), in both source and packaged mode.
- `packages/execution-router` answers "where does code run" on Windows, per #400: capability probing that assumes nothing, hot refresh, and a downgrade hook that tightens approval modes.
- Managed micromamba win-64 starter environments so direct execution can run Python out of the box.
- Unsandboxed execution is fail-closed: workspace allowlist, deny-all default network with audited refusals, persistent-shell guard, server-side approval tightening.
- POSIX behavior unchanged: sandboxed providers remain the Linux default and no posix path changes.

## Non-goals

- Provider B (the WSL sandbox plugin) itself — its rootfs, import state machine, and plugin center are a separate issue; here it stays a stub the router can register later.
- The remote provider (C) and macOS work.
- Any change to the existing `bubblewrap`/`seatbelt` enum semantics on Linux.
- Windows CI coverage (same gap as #482 — the evidence below is real-machine).

## Root decisions

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Routing layer placement | Layered **on top of** the sandbox enum, never inside it | #400's root decision: "new code is layered on top, so upstream merges continue to apply". The enum stays three-valued for sandboxed providers; `"none"` is the Windows direct-execution entry. |
| Startup orchestration | Windows-native `.mjs` chain (`stack-platform.mjs` platform dispatch + `jiuwenswarm.mjs` launcher) | Windows "covered without WSL being mandatory" (#400); a bash-free chain also survives GBK consoles and paths with spaces. |
| Scientific environments | micromamba win-64, starter environments pinned in the repo | The bundled starter environment is what makes M1's "never touching WSL" exit criterion reachable; on-demand-only would fail the ≤1 min first-run budget. |
| Unsandboxed semantics | Fail-closed everywhere, approval locked to ask-on-dangerous on downgrade | #400's security baseline: "treats anything indeterminate as unavailable rather than routing on unknown state"; the downgrade hook reuses setApprovalMode's Permission Epoch semantics so the lock is server-side. |
| Ephemeral vs persistent shell | Ephemeral shell through the environment's m2-bash; persistent sessions refuse without a sandbox | `run_shell` is bash-syntax and the model depends on it (#400: "the bundled starter environment includes a bash compatibility layer"); persistent workers are the sandbox's job, so they wait for Provider B. |

## Delivery

### Startup chain

`scripts/lib/stack-platform.mjs` (single platform dispatch), `scripts/jiuwenswarm.mjs` (wall-clock deadline, TCP-first probing, exec timeouts, heartbeat logging, first-start diagnostics, uv-trampoline bypass via `entry_points.txt`, lazy start, `SCIENCE_AGENT_ENVS_DIR`), `scripts/start-stack.mjs` (native orchestration incl. packaged-stack mode for the NSIS payload). Both launcher and platform layer carry `node:test` suites.

### Execution router

`packages/execution-router`: provider registry, capability probing that reuses the runner's `/execution-capability` and `/health` (no new wire format), and the provider-downgrade hook — when the sandbox is lost, every `always_allow` session is tightened to `ask_for_dangerous` through `setApprovalMode` + `publishApprovalModeChange`. Wired into api bootstrap and `POST /api/execution-provider`.

### Micromamba environments

Environment-store platform hooks (win-64 starter specs, interpreter paths, package-install guidance with win-64 alternatives), launcher preflight, `SandboxKind "none"` in the schema, and `scripts/fetch-managed-micromamba.mjs` win-64 pinning.

### Fail-closed permissions

Workspace whitelist via `SCIENCE_RUNNER_EXTRA_WORKSPACE_ROOTS`; the default network policy is a deny-all gateway with audited denials; persistent shell refuses without a sandbox; ephemeral shell runs through the environment's m2-bash; readiness reports `"none"` honestly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On a Windows host without WSL: `start-stack` brings port 4310 healthy natively, and the runner executes a Python task in the micromamba starter environment.
- [ ] The router probes capability at startup, caches it, refreshes on demand, and never routes on indeterminate state.
- [ ] Losing the sandbox tightens every `always_allow` session to `ask_for_dangerous`, server-side.
- [ ] Unsandboxed execution is confined to the workspace allowlist; default-policy network is deny-all with logged refusals.
- [ ] Persistent shell sessions fail closed outside a sandbox; ephemeral shell works through m2-bash.
- [ ] POSIX behavior unchanged: Linux defaults and all sandboxed paths identical to main.
- [ ] Launcher and platform-layer test suites run green on Windows.

## Open questions

1. Windows CI remains absent (same as #482's finding 4) — the real-machine evidence in the PR covers it for now; should a `windows-latest` job be added before Provider B lands?
2. `pnpm-lock.yaml` gains the `@sciencediscovery/execution-router` workspace dependency; builds must run before tests import `dist/`. Is the CI build step's ordering guaranteed on all jobs?
3. When Provider B (WSL plugin) lands, should its registration reuse this router's stub slot verbatim, or should the plugin center own registration?

## Related

- Parent: #400 (delivery design — implements its execution model, startup, and security baseline for Windows)
- Foundation: #639 (platform facades; this issue is stacked on it)
- Supersedes the runtime half of the closed #478
- Runner tree-kill behavior follows #482
643.title: [Feature] Windows runtime: native startup chain, execution routing, micromamba environments, and fail-closed permissions
